Full text

Abstract

An emerging set of hypotheses propose that overlap between task representations aids learning transfer but also invokes greater control demands during task-switching. A parallel line of research shows that we flexibly infer what is relevant to a task, and thus what forms task representations, by observing what events co-occur in time and space. Thus, varying how much two tasks are interleaved, which affects whether we can rely on temporal context to differentiate them (contextual clarity), could alter their representations and, in turn, how we generalise or switch between them. Across two experiments (N = 100 each), we tested whether contextual clarity during training impacts both learning transfer (Experiment One) and task-switching (Experiment Two). Participants searched grids of squares to find hidden targets.

Grid borders signalled two task-sets, each associated with different target locations. Participants then trained without these cues while task-sets switched pseudorandomly at one of two rates. The Stable group experienced rare switches (5%), whereas the Variable group experienced more frequent switches (30%). At test, explicit colour cues were reintroduced. Rare switching impaired transfer learning on a novel task that combined the trained tasks, but not on a task that replicated a single trained task (Experiment One).

However, the training regimen did not impact task-switching performance at test, where the switch rate increased to 50% (Experiment Two). These findings show that contextual clarity can dissociate task representations only at the expense of learning transfer, constraining theories regarding relationships between transfer and task-switching.

[div-01]

Human behaviour is remarkably flexible, in part because we leverage previously learned relationships to solve new problems. For example, we adapt faster to using a new phone if we can repurpose (transfer) our previous phone experiences (c.f. Garner et al., 2014 Garner et al., , 2016)). Although clearly beneficial, sharing learned information between tasks has also been proposed to induce performance costs: switching between two phones invokes greater control demands when performance relies on common information (see Musslick & Cohen, 2021, for a review). Despite suggestions that learning transfer and task-switching are commonly impacted by the extent of task overlap, we lack empirical tests in humans that probe the nature of this link. As context plays an important role in signalling which of the plethora of ongoing environmental signals are currently task-relevant-where more discernible contexts allow stronger dissociations between tasks that share common cues-(see Badre, 2025; Niv, 2019, for reviews) modulating contextual clarity may serve as a means to investigate the implied commonalities between learning transfer and task-switching.

To determine whether task-overlap commonly impacts learning transfer and task-switching, it is important to first consider what is encoded into the brain's representation of a task. A task representation (or task-set) is a model of the external and internal events that are relevant to a desired outcome (Duncan, 2025; Niv, 2019; Schneider & Logan, 2014; Vaidya & Badre, 2022). This may include environmental signals that denote the task context, such as a cue that indicates which set of stimulus-response rules are currently relevant (Musslick et al., 2019; Siqi-Liu et al., 2025; Vaidya et al., 2021; Wen et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2024); the stimulus-response rules themselves, such as which button to press in relation to a feature of the stimulus, and meta-task parameters, such as how ready one should be to adopt new stimulus-response rules (see Braem & Egner, 2018, for a review). Although task-relevant information could manifest in multiple formats in the brain (see Vaidya & Badre, 2022, for a review), evidence from monkey neurophsyiology and human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) suggests that task set elements are instantiated via activity in frontal-parietal cortices. Activity in these regions changes as the relevant learned relationships also change throughout a task (see Duncan, 2010 Duncan, , 2025;; Woolgar et al., 2016, for reviews), regardless of the identities of the learned relationships themselves. This motivates the question of what benefits might be gained when a common neural resource is used to implement sets across tasks.

One potential reason to deploy a common neural resource across multiple tasks is that it provides an opportunity to share information between task encounters. Indeed, a consistent finding across domains of human motor control (e.g. Douvis, 2005; Hernández-Davo et al., 2014), categorisation (e.g. Vukatana et al., 2015), visual perception (e.g. Manenti et al., 2023), and language acquisition (e.g. Barcroft & Sommers, 2005; Johns et al., 2016) is that training on variable samples (e.g. classifying many dogs vs many cats) promotes generalisation, compared to training on single samples (classifying one dog vs one cat). This suggests that exposure to varied instances enables identification of the key regularities that have driven successful performance between task encounters, that are invariant to the idiosyncrasies of each specific sample (see Raviv et al., 2022, for a review). Capitalising on between-sample regularities may not only support within-task generalisation, but also performance across tasks; neural networks that use the same hidden layer to encode multiple tasks show higher accuracy for each single task compared to networks that use a bespoke hidden layer for each task (see Caruana, 1997; Ruder, 2017, for reviews). This suggests that humans may similarly capitalise on regularities across tasks to support learning transfer. However, the circumstances in which regularities are exploited to support performance across tasks are only just beginning to be understood (Badre et al., 2021; Flesch et al., 2018 Flesch et al., , 2022;; Garner & Dux, 2015; Mueckstein et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2023). Indeed, humans often show negligible learning transfer between sets of stimulus-response rules that appear to share common properties (Garner et al., 2014 (Garner et al., , 2016;; Garner et al., 2015), where we might expect that learned information would be shared to support performance. For example, response time gains accrued from practising key press responses to visually presented letters do not transfer to benefit performance when the letter is spoken (Garner et al., 2016). This suggests that speeded stimulus-response performance may be a consequence of encoding the minimum task-specific attributes that support success. This encoding bias is evident early in learning; when a task switches without warning from reporting the colour of a letter among digit distractors to reporting the letter's identity, accuracy is substantially lower on the initial relative to subsequent identity trials, even after only ~11 colour trials. This is perhaps surprising given that in both cases, identifying a letter was key to performing the task (Chen & Wyble, 2016; O'Donnell & Wyble, 2021). Thus, there appear to be advantages to paring down the information encoded in a task-set that outweigh the potential disadvantages of increased reliance on a smaller number of features for performance.

One such advantage may be the reduction of conflict when performing multiple tasks. It is a robust finding that performance costs incurred from task switching-measured as slower and less accurate responses when switching between two sets of stimulus-response rules over consecutive trials, relative to repeating the same rules-are larger when common stimuli appear in both tasks, particularly when dimensions of those stimuli signal different responses in each task (see Kiesel et al., 2010; Koch et al., 2018, for reviews). An assumption underlying theories of multi-task performance is that the extent of task overlap intensifies the competition for some level of resources (Byrne & Anderson, 2001; Meyer & Kieras, 1997a , 1997b; Salvucci & Taatgen, 2008) or distributed representation (e.g. Feng et al., 2014; O'Reilly, 1998; Petri et al., 2021) that must be won by the current task in order to preserve performance. Although the consequences of this competition have been most extensively discussed in the context of multitasking and learning efficiency (see Garner & Dux, 2023; Musslick & Cohen, 2021, for reviews), it has also been assumed that stronger (competition-induced) prioritisation of the current task may act to make switching more difficult, either because prioritised activity persists, or because the competing task has been suppressed to a greater extent (Musslick & Cohen, 2019; Musslick et al., 2018; Ueltzhöffer et al., 2015).

Although there has been much debate into whether current demands for switching (indexed by the frequency of switching) motivate a momentary trade-off between conflict-proof performance and flexibility (e.g. Braem, 2017; Geddert & Egner, 2022; Mayr et al., 2013; Musslick et al., 2019; Nolden & Koch, 2023; Qiao et al., 2023), the assumed links between the extent of task-overlap, learning transfer, and task-switching performance remain to be explicitly tested. Specifically, we seek to understand whether tasks that reliably share more common properties both increase interference during task-switching, and induce more efficient transfer when acquiring a related task.

A challenge in testing this core assumption regarding the consequences of overlap between tasks is that we must determine what information is tagged as task-relevant in the first place (Duncan, 2025; Niv, 2019; Vaidya & Badre, 2022), to then judge how two tasks overlap. Context cues, such as time and place, can drive what stimulus features are included in a task-set, so that the same item evokes different responses based on expectations about a particular setting (Bouton, 2019; Gershman et al., 2013). For instance, the room in which a fear response was learned can re-evoke that response even after it has been extinguished elsewhere (Bouton, 2019). While we may wish away this particular example of context-specific learning, the ability to learn different rules for the same stimuli according to time or place is essential for making adaptive decisions-such as deciding how hard to run for a train based on whether they are following a peak or off-peak schedule. To decide, the learner must navigate covert transitions (e.g. the temporal shift from peak to off-peak) between situations with extensive stimulus overlap (e.g. the train station). Indeed, in the absence of explicit cues, individuals can often fail to detect that the task context has changed, and will make responses as if the previous/other context remains relevant, such as continuing to freeze to a sound even when it no longer predicts an electric shock (Bouton & Bolles, 1979; Gershman et al., 2013). From here on, we call such responses 'setting errors', as they suggest an erroneous carry-over of the wrong task-set onto current performance. Setting errors have been shown to reduce when greater surprise is invoked from the transition between task-contexts, such as when there is an abrupt and lasting change in stimulus-outcome relationships (Gershman et al., 2013), a low-probability change in task-relevant sensory-inputs (Gershman et al., 2014), or when transitions between tasks are rare compared to more frequent (Flesch et al., 2018; Qian & Aslin, 2014). These findings suggest that encountering an event which is more surprising, given recent experiences, serves to mark a change in context (increases contextual clarity), which, in turn, allows greater dissociation of task-sets pre-and post-surprise. Indeed, it has been proposed that when covert transitions between task-states are unsurprising, between-context events are attributed to a single cause or bound to a single memory (e.g. Gershman et al., 2013 Gershman et al., , 2017;; Niv, 2019; Qian & Aslin, 2014; Qian et al., 2016). Therefore, manipulations of covert transitions between task-states, such as whether task-switches occur rarely vs frequently, should modify contextual clarity, and consequently impact how much dissociation occurs between task-sets. In turn, the degree to which task sets dissociate or overlap should impact learning transfer and task-switching.

As well as intermixing tasks to induce overlap, we can harness setting errors to assess how each person has responded to a particular sequence of tasks. Although it remains to be determined whether setting errors reflect integration of the incorrect stimulus-response rule into an established task-set (Gershman et al., 2013 (Gershman et al., , 2014)), a lapse into activating the wrong task-set (Woolgar et al., 2019), or an increased propensity to switch tasks (Braem, 2017), they are a useful instance of performance interference because we can attribute them to a specific task-set. Therefore, situations that reliably elicit setting errors may provide a useful proxy for the extent to which task-sets have been dissociated (or not). A recent study from Garner, Leow, et al. (2024) demonstrates a way to systematically elicit setting errors. Participants were required to perform two tasks, each of which involved searching a four-by-four grid of squares for a hidden target. Participants gazed at squares to "open" them to find the target. If the fixated location was the target location, it was revealed; if not, the square turned dark for a moment to signal an empty space.

The grid was bordered by one of two colours, and the colour signalled in which subset of locations the target could be found, with four squares assigned uniquely to each subset. Thus, on each trial, the colour cue signalled which four locations were task relevant. When the tasks were performed with a 50% probability of a task-switch, participants were more likely to perform a setting error (that is, select a square that belonged to the wrong task) than they were to make a random error (select a square from neither task). Thus, in this paradigm, locations relevant to another task served as a source of cross-task interference, suggesting that setting errors reflect the relationship between the tasks, and not just the overall level of focus. Promoting contextual clarity by reducing the rate of switching may serve to attenuate setting errors, which in turn can be interpreted as evidence for increased dissociation between task-sets. Further, by constructing tasks consisting of multiple stimulus-response associations, such as visiting the four locations specific to each task (Garner, Leow, et al., 2024), it is also possible to generate novel tasks that overlap in varying degrees with what has been previously learned by combining subsets of each task; for example, by using two locations from each learned task to form a novel set of four. Thus, this paradigm offers the opportunity not only to investigate whether contextual clarity during training modulates interference between task-sets, but also to determine how such training impacts both learning transfer and task-switching. Here, across two experiments, we examine how contextual clarity during training influences these two hallmarks of flexibility. In each experiment, participants completed a training regimen of the task described above. The probability of a task switch could be low/rare [p(switch)=.05, Stable group], or higher/more frequent [p(switch)=.3, Variable group]. We hypothesised that low rates of switching during this training period would result in greater dissociation between task-sets, as rare switches should serve to better segregate the two task contexts. In contrast, more frequent switching should result in task-sets that are more highly associated, either because frequent switching results in an amalgamation of task-sets or because the task-sets are more strongly associated by an increased expectation of the need to switch between them. Therefore, across both experiments, we anticipated that the Variable group would mix up locations from both tasks more often than the Stable group.

In Experiment One, after this training, participants completed two learning transfer tasks, each presented using a grid with a novel coloured border. One task was an identical mapping of a previously learned task (Identity task), and the second was a combination of subsets of learned tasks, where two target locations were taken from each (Mixed task). Performance of this latter task requires connecting elements of task-sets. Thus, task-sets that are more highly associated -as would be expected when frequently switching during training -should be at an advantage for supporting performance in the mixed situation, relative to task-sets that have been more greatly dissociated via the contextual clarity attained with rare switching. In contrast, connecting elements of task-sets is not required (and could potentially be detrimental) when completing the Identity task. Therefore, we anticipated that the Variable group should perform better on the Mixed task (and perhaps worse on the Identity task) relative to the Stable group.

Experiment Two followed the same method as Experiment One, except that instead of a learning transfer task, participants completed a test phase where the trained tasks were performed under conditions of increased task-switching probability [p(switch)=.5]. If task-switching demands are attributable to interference between task-sets, then setting errors should be greater for switch trials, compared to trials where there has been no switch (stay trials). If training modulates the extent to which task-sets are associated, then this should impact the difference in setting errors between switch and stay trials.

Specifically, if frequent switching during training results in greater associations between task-sets, then the Variable group should show more setting errors than the Stable group, particularly on switch trials, when competition between task-sets should be highest. However, as the Variable group would have practised switching between tasks more frequently than the Stable group, the Variable group could show reduced response-time costs when switching (cf. Braem, 2017; Geddert & Egner, 2024; Musslick et al., 2019). The key question concerns whether changes to behaviour occur concomitantly with inverse changes in setting errors, and whether the conditions that drive improved learning transfer in Experiment One correspond to increased setting errors during switching in Experiment Two.

Experiment One

Method Participants

Participants were 118 healthy adults (age = 20.9±5.72, six unreported; 27 reported their sex as being best described as male, 91 reported as female; from 5 options: male/female/intersex/other/prefer not to say) recruited from the paid and course-credit participant pools at the University of New South Wales.

The study was approved by the UNSW Human Research Ethics Committee (approval number 6341). All participants were informed about the study's design and gave written consent before beginning the study.

Participants were awarded course credit or cash (AUD30) for participating, and a performance-based cash bonus (AUD10-20). The testing session took up to 90 minutes to complete.

Stimuli and Materials

Stimuli were grids of four by four squares, shown on a light grey background (HSL: 0 • , 0%, 78%).

Grids appeared centrally and measured 8.36 degrees of visual angle at an 80 cm viewing distance. Grids were shown with a grey or coloured border (HSL: [grey] 0 • , 0%, 62.75%; [green] 162 • , 72%, 36%; [orange] 26 • , 98%, 43%; [purple] 244 • , 31%, 57%; [pink] 321 • , 64%, 45%). Squares were medium grey by default (HSL: 0 • , 0%, 37.65%), and dark grey when selected with the left mouse button (HSL: 0 • , 0%, 7.84%), unless the square was the target, where clicking it revealed an image of an animal (Fig 1A). Animal images were randomly drawn from a set of 100 that were downloaded from the internet (available in the https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16623762).

Procedure

Participants were seated at a desk in a quiet booth with a viewing distance of approximately 67 cm. They completed three experimental phases: a task acquisition phase, a training phase, and a learning transfer test phase.

Task Acquisition

The goal of the task acquisition phase was to ensure that participants could perform both tasks with high accuracy prior to the training phase. Participants were instructed that their task was to find an animal target that was hiding behind one of the squares, and that they should use the mouse to click on squares to find the target. Next, they completed five practice trials where the grid of squares was presented with a dark grey border. The location of the target was drawn randomly from the 16 squares for these five trials. The trial began with presentation of the grid of squares, presented in the default grey surrounded by a dark grey border. If a non-target square was selected then the square turned dark grey for the duration of the selection before reverting to the default colour. If the target square was selected then the target was presented for a total of 500 ms, including the duration for which the mouse button was depressed. The next trial began once the square reverted back to default grey.

After the five practice trials, participants were told that they would now see the squares surrounded by a coloured border, and that the colour signalled a specific house. Participants were also informed that their task was now to learn to find the animal target in four moves or fewer. They were also informed that if they found the target in four moves or fewer, then a tone would be played that signalled their success. Tones were taken from a 2000 ms piano arpeggio where the number of tones played mapped inversely to the number of moves taken to find the target (for example, a target found in one move elicited four tones; a target found in four moves elicited one tone).

Participants then performed the task with the first coloured border, which was drawn pseudorandomly from the four colours listed above. This mapping of coloured border to four target locations were their Task A. The four target locations were pseudorandomly selected across participants, with the constraint that one target location fell in each quadrant of the grid, with one and only one target in a corner and one and only one target in the inner quadrant of the grid (see Fig 1B for an example).

Participants completed Task A for a minimum of 40 trials and then continued until they met the criterion of finding the target within four moves for at least 9 of the preceding 10 trials (so a perfect performer could complete the task within 50 trials), or until 200 trials had been completed. On completion of Task A, participants were instructed that they would now see a new coloured border which signalled that the animals had moved to a new house, and that they would be found in four new locations (Task B). Task B locations were pseudorandomly chosen according to the same criteria as for Task A, with the additional constraint that no locations could overlap with those selected for Task A (see Fig 1B). They completed Task B according to the same accuracy criterion as set for Task A. Participants were then instructed that they would complete each task once more, and completed a further block of 40 trials in Task A, followed by a block of 40 trials in Task B. Participants who failed to find the target within four moves on a minimum of 80% of trials for each task were excluded from the remainder of the experiment (18 participants: age = 24.4±9.9, two unreported; four male, 14 female). Thus, 100 participants were included in the remaining phases (age = 20.3±4.49, four unreported; 23 male, 77 female). We do not analyse the Task Acquisition data here as participants were selected according to specific accuracy criterion in this phase. However, figures depicting accuracy for each Group and Task are presented in the online notebook of results, and the link for this notebook is listed at the beginning of the Statistical Design section.

Training

The goal of the training stage was to manipulate how frequently the tasks were switched between over time, in the absence of explicit cues that instruct which task is currently relevant. More frequent switching between latent states has been argued to reduce contextual clarity, and thereby reduce the likelihood that they are represented separately (e.g. Qian & Aslin, 2014). Note that this manipulation is distinct to classic manipulations of switch-rate used in task-switching studies (e.g. Fröber & Dreisbach, 2017; Geddert & Egner, 2024; Musslick et al., 2019), as those studies examine the impact of increasing switch-rates when explicit cues unambiguously signal which task should be performed on any given trial.

Thus, participants were informed that their task was to continue to find the targets in four moves or fewer. Further, they were informed that they would no longer see the coloured borders, and that now the house could switch on any trial. The coloured borders were removed to reduce the explicit and clear dissociation between the two tasks; switching between two tasks with clear task cues could dissociate task-sets more when frequently switching between the two, which would undermine our contextual clarity manipulation.

Participants were also informed that on any given trial the task was always more likely to stay the same than to switch. Note that if the probability of a switch is less than p=.5 (as was the case for all participants during the training phase), then the optimal strategy is to exhaust the potential target locations from the task associated with the location at which the previous target was found, before switching to the other task (e.g., after finding a target at a location associated with Task A, the best strategy is to search all Task A target locations, and if they are all empty, then switch to searching Task B target locations). All participants completed 160 trials of Task A and 160 trials of Task B.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two training groups. For the Stable group, the probability of a task-switch was p=.05, for the Variable group the probability was p=.3 (Fig 1C). Trial sequences were pseudorandomly generated with the constraint that an equal number of Task A and Task B trials must be completed over the course of training.

To balance explicit feedback between the two groups, a proportion of trials were randomly allocated as feedback trials. Participants were informed that now they would hear the performance-contingent tones on only a subset of trials (reward trials), and that the tone signalled how many points they had won. Points were converted to a cash bonus at the end of the session (10-20AUD).

Only Stay (non-switch) trials were selected as reward trials, as this guarantees points under the optimal performance strategy. Further, the number of trials randomly allocated as reward trials was equivalent to 50% of the Stay trials experienced by the Variable group, thus equating the number of possible reward trials between the two groups.

Learning Transfer Test

After training, participants completed two blocks of 40 transfer trials. A new coloured border was used for each block (randomly selected from the remaining two possible border colours). Participants were informed that the new coloured borders represented moving to a new house, and that they may be able to
