Transparency and Openness

All experimental protocols/presentation code was written for Matlab R2023a using Psychtoolbox v3.0.19, and the code is available from the https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16623762. Data were preprocessed and analysed using bespoke scripts written in R. Data are available https://osf.io/4ehry/overview (Barnes et al., 2026). Preprocessing scripts are available https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16760165 and the data analysis can be reproduced at the online notebook https://garner-code.github.io/context-clarity_produce-results/. Neither the study nor the analysis plan were preregistered. No specific reporting guidelines were followed.

Statistical Design

Training

Task Jumps. First, we quantified the extent to which participants pre-emptively moved back and forth between Task A and Task B over the course of a single trial during the training phase (task jumps).

More frequent task jumps means that a participant was more likely to click both Task A and Task B locations while performing either task. Task jumps were defined as the number of times participants moved between Task A and Task B locations over the course of finding a single target (completing a single trial).

The first move on any trial was assessed relative to the location of the target on the previous trial. For example, if the participant previously found a target at location A 4 , and (unknown to them) the next target was at location A 3 (making this a Stay trial since the current trial and the previous trial were both from Task A), the selections A 1 , A 2 , B 1 , B 2 , A 3 would incur a task jump score of two. If the target on the previous trial was at location B 1 , the same selections on the current trial would incur a task jump score of three. We counted task jumps separately for each trial and averaged within Stay and Switch trials. As Switch trials require a task jump to find the target, a value of one was subtracted from Switch trials prior to averaging to equate the scale between trial types.

General Errors.

General errors were quantified as the proportion of selected squares that were relevant to neither Task A nor Task B, relative to the total number of squares selected on that trial.

Proportion of general errors was averaged within Stay and Switch trials for each participant. General errors assess the extent to which participants have failed to maintain task-specific behaviours, with an increase in general errors suggesting that participants are less able to recall target locations for either task, or an increase in carelessness.

Task jumps and general errors were both analysed using a 2 (Group: Stable vs Variable) x 2 (Trial Type: Stay vs Switch) mixed ANOVA design. For each dependent variable, a priori comparisons were made for the main effect of Group (Stable vs Variable), the main effect of Trial Type (Stay vs Switch), and the Group x Trial Type interaction. Follow up post-hoc contrasts implemented a Scheffé adjustment procedure controlling for family-wise type 1 error rate. The task jumps and general errors distributions both showed skewness and outliers. We therefore confirmed that any significant (and non-significant) effects held regardless of whether or not we transformed the data (for these and all remaining analyses).

However, we report only the results using the non-transformed data for ease of interpretability. The use of the parametric ANOVA approach with the current data is warranted, as type 1 error rates remain at 5% when there are violations of normality assumptions (Blanca et al., 2023; Schmider et al., 2010), and group differences in variances larger than those observed here (see Table 2 of Glass et al., 1972), for as long as group sizes are equal, as is the case in the current work. Further, ANOVA has been shown to perform comparably to non-parametric alternatives with group sizes equal to the n = 50 as used here (Marcinko, 2014). Last, to validate our assumptions, we used the current data to simulate the robustness of ANOVA when the null hypothesis is true. Starting with the task jumps variable, we randomly assigned the data points to the Group x Trial Type conditions (without replacement) over 1000 iterations. The resulting type 1 errors were at 5% for both main effects and the interaction (all p(p < .05) = 0.05). We repeated this procedure for the most positively and negatively skewed dependent variables from the dataset, and found type 1 error rates ranging from 4% to 5%. This validates that ANOVA is appropriate to use with the current data. We do note that the skew of the data may drive some bias in the reported effect sizes (generalised η² Garner, Nolan, et al., 2024; Troncoso Skidmore & Thompson, 2013). However, we report generalised η² to facilitate comparisons with other studies, as recommended (Bakeman, 2005) and as would be required to garner a more precise effect size estimate over cumulative studies.

Learning Transfer Test

Task Knowledge Onset. The primary goal of the analysis of learning transfer performance was to quantify at which point participants knew the task well enough to perform it accurately. To achieve this, we implemented a previously published Bayesian algorithm (Maggi et al., 2024) that quantifies the certainty that an individual is following a predefined strategy or mode of behaviour. Behaviour is coded on each trial as evidence for (1) or against (0) a given mode (or as an absence of evidence). This evidence is used to update a Beta distribution quantifying the probability that the mode of interest governed performance on that trial. To allow for change in the mode that governs behaviour, the prior evidence is decayed by a constant factor (γ) just before the update. On any given trial, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) of the distribution captures the probability that that mode is governing behaviour, whereas the precision (inverse of the variance) gives the certainty of the probability estimate. A separate Beta distribution is used for each mode of interest. A particular mode is dominant when the associated MAP exceeds the MAPs associated with the remaining modes; precision information can be added to refine inferences when required (not required in the current study).

To implement this algorithm, we first defined four modes of behaviour that could govern performance at any given moment of the learning transfer test; participants could know one [K1], two [K2], three [K3], or four [K4] of the possible target locations that were relevant to their current task. Next, for each participant and learning transfer task (Identity or Mixed) we applied a sliding window of four selections to the selection vector for the whole task, moving forward one element at a time. The number of target-relevant locations (for that task) that occurred within the window was taken as evidence for the corresponding mode, and all other modes were scored zero for that trial. For example, if three out of four of the selections were locations where a target could appear, then the K3 mode was scored one, while the remaining modes were scored zero. We then updated the associated Beta distributions, beginning with uniform priors and using a default γ=0.9 (Maggi et al., 2024). This provided a time series of MAPs that quantified the likelihood that participants were in each mode at any given point. Last, we found the earliest point at which the K4 MAP both exceeded the other MAPs and continued to exceed them for the rest of the task. We took this to be the moment at which full task knowledge was acquired for that task.

Accuracy. To corroborate the task knowledge onset analysis, we also measured overall accuracy on each transfer task. Accuracy was computed as the number of target-relevant location selections on a trial, relative to the total number of location selections on that trial. Accuracy was averaged over trials for each participant and transfer task.

Setting Errors. Setting errors were computed to determine whether participants applied previously learned behaviours to perform the transfer task when those behaviours were no longer relevant.

For example, if the first discovered target location in a transfer task was from Task A, a participant could enact all Task A behaviours, or only the Task A behaviours that have revealed a target in the transfer task.

Enacting all Task A behaviours would facilitate performance in the Identity task, but could delay task knowledge onset and reduce accuracy in the Mixed task. We computed setting errors as the number of times a location was selected that belonged to Task A or B but that was not included in the current transfer task, relative to all selections made on that trial (i.e. relevant for the current task-context, relevant for another task-context, and those that were never task-relevant), averaged across trials.

General Errors.

General errors were calculated as in the training stage, and quantified the proportion of selections relevant to neither task, relative to all other possible selections. Therefore, general errors were used to determine whether any group differences in transfer performance were due to one group more often selecting locations unrelated to Task A or B.

Task knowledge onset, accuracy, and setting errors were each analysed using a 2 (Group: Stable vs Variable) x 2 (Transfer Condition: Identity vs Mixed) mixed ANOVA design, using the same follow-up comparison procedure as defined above for the training stage data.

Transparency and openness.

Results

Training

Task Jumps

As anticipated, the training manipulation affected behavioural mixing of the two task sets (Fig 3A). This was demonstrated by a significant Group x Trial Type interaction (F(1,98)=24.36, η² =0.008, p<.001). Specifically, the Stable group showed comparable numbers of task jumps between Stay (M=0.35, SE=0.14, 95% CI[0.08,0.63]) and Switch trials (M=0.44, SE=0.13, 95% CI[0.18,0.71], t(98) = 1.83, p=0.28). In contrast, the Variable group showed more task jumps on Stay trials (M=1.08, SE=0.14, 95% CI[0.8,1.35]) compared to Switch trials (M=0.82, SE=0.13, 95% CI[0.56,1.09], t(98)=-5.15, p<.001). The Variable group also showed more task jumps compared to the Stable group within Stay trials (t(98)=3.67, p<.001). The two groups did not statistically differ in task jumps on Switch trials (t(98)=1.99, p=0.2).

This indicates that the Variable group mixed the behaviours relevant to Task A and Task B on Stay trials, when they only needed to perform one of the two tasks. In contrast, the Stable group showed less mixing, or a greater separation of behaviours relevant to Task A and Task B trials. We return to consider the underlying processes in the General Discussion.

General Errors

The increased mixing of tasks demonstrated by the Variable group was not driven by a general impairment in performing task-relevant behaviours (Fig 3C) nor was there a significant Group x Trial Type interaction (both ps > 0.08). Thus, the groups could not be differentiated by their rates of task-irrelevant behaviours during training.

Learning Transfer Test

Having established that the Variable group showed a greater mixing of behaviours relevant to Task A and Task B during training compared to the Stable group, we next sought to determine the impact on learning transfer performance.

Task knowledge onset. Task knowledge onset was estimated for 86 participants -the remaining 14 participants did not demonstrate evidence that they had learned the four new locations by the end of one of the tasks. Of these 14, 9 were from the Stable group. A binomial probability test showed that the probability of non-learners belonging to the Stable group (versus the Variable group) was not significantly different from 0.5 (p=0.42).

Task knowledge onset is presented in Fig 4A. As expected, both groups took longer to learn the four locations for the Mixed condition (onset window M=67.12, SE=3.61, 95% CI[59.94, 74.31]) compared to the Identity condition (M=50.04, SE=4.14, 95% CI[41.8, 58.27]). This was supported by a main effect of Transfer Condition (F(1, 84)=11.24, η² =0.054, p<.001). In line with the hypothesis that switching during training modulates the separability of task information, there was a significant Group x Transfer Condition interaction (F(1, 84)=4.79, η² =0.024, p=0.031). Follow-up tests showed that the Stable group took longer to learn the Mixed transfer task (M=72.54, SE=5.23, 95% CI[62.14,82.93]), compared to the Identity task (M=44.29, SE=5.99, 95% CI[32.37,56.21], t(84) = 3.83, p<.001).

In contrast, the Variable group did not show a significant difference between the Mixed (M=61.71, SE=4.99, 95% CI[51.79, 71.63]) and Identity tasks (M=55.78, SE=5.72, 95% CI[44.4, 67.16], p=1). The two groups were not statistically different for either the Mixed or Identity conditions (both ps > 0.55). These results suggest that rare switching during training reduced the mixing of behaviours from Task A and Task B, making it hard for the Stable group to discover target locations in the Mixed transfer task. Accuracy. The results of the accuracy data mirrored the knowledge onset data (Fig 4B). Again, a significant Group x Transfer Condition interaction demonstrated that training impacted performance on the transfer tasks (F(1, 98)=4.87, η² =0.015, p=0.03). Post-hoc follow up tests showed that the Stable group were less accurate in the Mixed condition (M=0.89, SE=0.01, 95% CI[0.86, 0.91]), compared to the Identity condition (M=0.94, SE=0.01, 95% CI [0.92, 0.96], t(98) = -4.12, p<.001). In contrast, the difference between the Mixed and Identity condition was not statistically significant for the Variable group (Mixed M=0.91, SE=0.01, 95%CI [0.89, 0.94], Identity M=0.93, SE=0.01, 95 % CI[0.9, 0.95], p=1). The two groups were not statistically different for either the Mixed or Identity conditions (both ps > 0.55). In line with the knowledge onset data, these results suggest that rare switches during training, which reduced behavioural mixing of Task A and Task B locations, prepared the Stable group for Identity but not Mixed transfer.

Setting Errors.

Next, we determined whether group accuracy differences could be due to an application of behaviours from Task A and B that were no longer relevant for the transfer task. Setting errors quantify the proportion of responses that were from a previously learned task (A or B), when those locations were no longer relevant (Fig 4C). In support of the idea that such a strategy may have delayed knowledge onset in the Mixed condition, both groups showed increased setting errors for the Mixed condition (Stable M=0.15, SE=0.01, 95% CI[0.12, 0.18], Variable M=0.12, SE=0.01, 95% CI[0.1, 0.15]) compared to the Identity condition (Stable M=0.08, SE=0.01, 95% CI[0.05, 0.1], Variable M=0.09, SE=0.01, 95% CI[0.07, 0.12]), as demonstrated by a main effect of Transfer Condition (F(1, 98)=21.34, η² =0.073, p<.001).

Although there was a numerical trend towards this difference being larger for the Stable compared to the Variable group (Fig 4C), the interaction was not statistically significant (F(1, 98)=3.56, η² =0.013, p=0.062). Thus, both groups showed a greater reliance on learned but now irrelevant behaviours during learning of the Mixed transfer task than the Identity transfer task.

General Errors.

Last, we sought to determine whether group differences in transfer performance could be attributed to the Variable group learning to try more locations in general. It could be that this group was more ready to try any location on the transfer tasks, which could confer an advantage for knowledge onset in the Mixed condition. For example, if a participant had learned that location A 1 was relevant for the new task, having the strategy of trying any location could lead to an earlier discovery that a B location is relevant, relative to a participant who pursued the remaining A locations. We therefore calculated general errors -the proportion of location selections that are relevant to neither Task A nor Task B, averaged across trials (Fig 4D). Although general errors increased slightly from the Identity condition (M=0.06, SE=0.01, 95% CI[0.05, 0.08]) to the Mixed condition (M=0.07, SE=0.01, 95% CI[0.06, 0.09], F(1, 98)=4.2, η² =0.008, p=0.043), this increase did not differ between the groups (p=0.125), nor did the groups differ overall (p=0.908). Therefore, the observed group differences cannot be explained by the Variable group indiscriminately selecting more locations.

Discussion

We investigated whether rare or frequent switches between tasks during training modulates the transfer of learned behaviours to novel tasks. We observed that a 'Stable' group, which switched rarely between tasks during training, fared more poorly on a transfer task that combined subsets of behaviours from both trained tasks, as compared to a transfer task that applied one of the trained tasks in its entirety.

Further, this difference was not observed for the 'Variable' group, which switched between tasks more frequently during training. This suggests that rare switching drives a stronger dissociation between task contexts, either by modifying the underlying representations of task rules (Flesch et al., 2018; Gershman et al., 2013; Niv, 2019), or the propensity to switch between sets of task rules (Braem, 2017; Geddert & Egner, 2024; Musslick et al., 2019).

A possible alternative explanation for the current findings is that, as more frequent switching is intrinsically harder than rare switching, the Variable group may have become more error prone during training. This may have primed them to try any location in the transfer tasks, potentially offering an advantage for the Mixed condition. The analysis of general errors in both the training and transfer stages argues against this account. First, the Stable and Variable groups made low and comparable numbers of general errors during the training phase, demonstrating that the Variable group did not become more error prone. Further, this lack of group difference in general errors carried over into the transfer phase, suggesting that both groups used comparable amounts of previous task knowledge to learn the transfer tasks. Thus, the results are likely due to group differences in how they applied task knowledge to the transfer stage, rather than any difference in how well they knew the trained tasks.

The current results show that training on tasks with rare switches reduces the likelihood of recombining the tasks during a transfer phase, suggesting that contextual clarity induces greater dissociation in the information encoded into the underlying task representations. One potential benefit of such a dissociation is reduced task-competition, which may result in reduced control demands when switching between tasks (Musslick & Cohen, 2021; Musslick et al., 2019). In Experiment Two, we sought evidence of such a relationship, by substituting the learning transfer test stage from Experiment One with a task-switching stage. If the conditions that impair learning transfer performance also serve to reduce conflict between tasks, then the Stable group should show reduced cross-task interference when switching, compared to the Variable group.

Experiment Two

In Experiment Two, we tested whether the Stable group, whose training may have resulted in more strongly dissociated task-sets, would find it easier to switch between the trained tasks than the Variable group, whose training may have resulted in greater associations between the trained tasks. This difference in switching ability should be most visible when participants are required to switch between tasks rapidly and frequently. Therefore, in Experiment Two, participants completed the same training regimen as Experiment One, but in place of the learning transfer test phase, they completed a task-switching test, where the probability of a switch was p=.5 for both groups.

Method Participants

Participants were 126 healthy adults (age 19.5±2.70, age unreported for four; 38 reported their sex best described as male, 84 were best described as female, four use another term) recruited from the paid and course-credit participant pools at the University of New South Wales. Twenty-six participants were excluded following the acquisition phase (age = 20.1±2.83; eight male, 18 female), leaving 100 participants (age = 19.3±2.66, four unreported; 30 male, 66 female, four use another term) for the remaining two phases. The study was approved by the UNSW Human Research Ethics Committee (approval number 6341). All participants provided written consent before the session began. Participants received AUD30 or course credit for their time, and a performance-related bonus (AUD10-20). The testing session lasted ~90 minutes.

Procedure

The task acquisition and training phases were identical to Experiment One.

Task-Switching Test

In contrast to Experiment One, the training phase was now followed by a task-switching test. The coloured borders (signifying which task was currently in effect) that were absent during the training phase were reintroduced for the task-switching test. Further, for both groups, the probability of a task-state switch increased to p=.5 (Fig 5), and the target was now presented only for as long as the mouse button was depressed (instead of for up to 500 ms). The trial sequence for the task-switching test was pseudorandomly generated for each participant so that it consisted of 80 Task A trials and 80 Task B trials while keeping the probability of a switch at p=.5. Participants were informed that they would now complete the task one more time with the coloured borders returned, and that they should perform each trial as quickly and accurately as possible.

Figure 5

Task-switching test phase of Experiment Two. The coloured borders returned, and the task-state switch probability was increased to 50%.

Trials

Statistical Design

The analysis of the training phase data followed the procedure of Experiment One.

Task-Switching Test

We derived measures to assess task-switching performance, based on accuracy, response time (RT), setting errors, and general errors. As the colour cues were available during this phase, Stay and Switch trials can be compared directly.

Response Time (RT).

We assumed that cross-task interference would impact the time taken to select the first correct target location, on trials where the first selection was correct. We calculated the average first correct RT for each participant and task state condition (Stay vs Switch). We excluded any RT > 4 seconds, to remove unrealistic values. Outliers were defined as RTs > 2.5 standard deviations from the mean for each participant and task state condition. Outliers constituted <2% of the total data.

Accuracy.

Accuracy was calculated as in Experiment One.

Setting Errors.

Setting errors were defined as location selections that were relevant to the task not currently presented (that is, Task B location selections while performing Task A), relative to all location selections. Note that a distinction can be made between setting errors that occur prior to the first accurate selection compared to those occurring later in the trial. The former, when occurring on switch trials, would reflect a failure to update to the current task state, whereas the latter reflect ongoing interference from the currently-irrelevant task that is not due to carry-over effects from the last trial. Although we calculated both of these types of setting errors, analysis revealed the same pattern of results (see the https://garner-code.github.io/context-clarity_produce-results/ for details), so we collapse across them here. Thus, total setting errors were counted per trial relative to all selections, and were averaged across trials for each participant and condition.

General Errors.

General errors were calculated as in Experiment One.

All data were analysed using a 2 (Group) x 2 (Trial Type: Stay vs Switch) design, using the same follow-up comparison procedure as Experiment One.

Results

Training

Task Jumps

In line with Experiment One, the training manipulation affected behavioural mixing of the two task sets (Fig 3B).

The difference between Stay and Switch trials was different between groups, as demonstrated by a significant Group x Trial Type interaction (F(1,98)=16.54, η² =0.01, p<.001). Post-hoc tests showed that the Stable group performed fewer task jumps on Stay trials (M=0.33, SE=0.14, 95% CI[0.05, 0.61]) compared to Switch trials (M=0.6, SE=0.16, [0.28, 0.92], t(98) = 3.67, p<.001), whereas the Variable group showed the opposite pattern (Stay M=1.22, SE=0.14, 95% CI[0.94, 1.5], Switch M=1.06, SE=0.16, 95% CI[0.75, 1.38], t(98)=-2.08, p=0.16). Note that these results follow the same numerical pattern as Experiment One, but differ in that the difference between Stay and Switch trials did not reach statistical significance for the Stable group in Experiment One. Post-hoc tests also showed that, in line with Experiment One, the Variable group performed more task jumps than the Stable group on Stay trials (t(98)=4.45, p<.001), and the two groups did not differ significantly on Switch trials (t(98)=2.04, p=0.18). Thus, the Variable group showed an increased mixing of Task A and Task B behaviours on Stay trials, compared to Switch trials, and compared to the Stable group, that replicates the findings from Experiment One.

General Errors

In line with Experiment One, general errors were low overall, and occurred more on Switch trials In line with Experiment One, the interaction between Group x Trial Type was not significant (p=0.22, Fig 3D).

Task-Switching Test

Having broadly replicated the impact of Stable and Variable training on the propensity to mix

Task A and Task B behaviours during the training phase (when colour borders explicitly signalling the current task were absent), we next determined the impact of training on task-switching performance in the presence of the colour borders.

Response Time

First, we assessed the influence of training on RTs, defined as the time until the first selection on a given trial, on trials where the first selection was correct for the cued task set.

Switching between task sets elicited performance costs; RTs were slower on Switch (Stable M=1.18, SE=0.04, 95% CI[1.11, 1.26], Variable M=1.14, SE=0.04, 95% CI[1.06, 1.21]) compared to Stay trials (Stable M=0.77, SE=0.02, 95% CI[0.72, 0.82], Variable M=0.76, SE=0.02, 95% CI[0.71, 0.81], F(1, 98)= 304.86, 0.417, p<.001). Both the main effect of Group and the Group x Trial Type interaction were not significant (both ps > 0.215, Fig 6A), failing to support the hypothesis that the Stable group would show reduced switched costs relative to the Variable group. Accuracy The RT findings were not due to a speed/accuracy trade-off. Both groups showed poorer accuracy on Switch trials (Stable M=0.92, SE=0.02, 95% CI[0.89, 0.96], Variable M=0.88, SE=0.02, 95% CI[0.84, 0.92]) compared to Stay trials (Stable M=0.95, SE=0.02, 95% CI[0.92, 0.99], Variable M=0.91, SE=0.02, 95% CI[0.87, 0.95], F(1, 98)= 81.51, 0.013, p<.001, Fig 6B). Neither the main effect of Group nor the Group x Trial Type interaction were significant (both ps > 0.098).

Setting Errors

In line with the RT data, setting errors were higher on Switch trials ( Stable M=0.01, SE=0.01, 95% CI[-0.01, 0.03], Variable M=0.04, SE=0.01, 95% CI[0.02, 0.06], p=0.104, Fig 6D).

Further, the Group by Trial Type interaction was not significant (p=0.702). There was a numerical suggestion that the Variable group may show higher general errors overall, but this interaction did not achieve significance (p=0.057).

Discussion

In Experiment Two, we sought to determine whether a training regimen that hampers learning transfer also reduces task-switching costs. Despite the clear impact of training on learning transfer in Experiment One, we did not observe any impact of training on the magnitude of switch costs in Experiment Two. This was observed even though the test phase manipulations elicited robust switch costs across the key behavioural measures of RT, accuracy, and setting errors. This is perhaps surprising, given that task-switching was fundamental to the training regimen (albeit without explicit task set cues), with the Variable group switching more frequently than the Stable group. We return to this point in the General Discussion. These results show that learning transfer and task-switching are not tightly bound together, as the conditions that limited learning transfer did not improve task-switching. Thus, in this instance, we were unable to observe the previously hypothesised relationship between learning a new task and switching between learned tasks, despite proposals that they both rely to some extent on how much the learned task representations overlap (Musslick & Cohen, 2021; Musslick et al., 2019).

In general, the impact of the training regimen replicated the results of Experiment One, allowing us to compare the test phases of both experiments. The Variable group once again mixed Task A and Task B behaviours more on Stay compared to Switch trials, and compared to the Stable group, within the training phase. Thus, the training regimen yielded the same pattern of behaviour across both experiments.

There were some small differences in performance during training between the experiments, which do not undermine comparison of learning transfer and task-switching outcomes. Specifically, in Experiment Two, the Stable group showed significantly more task jumps on Switch compared to Stay trials during the training phase. In Experiment One, the Stable group showed numerically more task jumps on Switch compare to Stay trials, but the difference was not statistically significant. A further departure is that, in Experiment Two, the Variable group showed an increase in general errors during training compared to the Stable group, which could suggest that the Variable group lost task knowledge during training. However, the difference was numerically very small (error difference ≈ .03-.04). General errors did not differ between Stay and Switch trials during the test phase, suggesting that the tendency to make a location selection relevant to neither task played a minimal role in the key cognitive processes tapped by the test phase.

These minor departures between groups during training should only have served to exacerbate group differences in the task-switching test, if they were driven by general task confusion; yet such group differences were not observed.

Experiment Two used the same large sample size as used in Experiment One (N =100).

Importantly, this sample size was sufficient to detect the influence of training on learning transfer performance, yet no training group differences were observed when assessing task switch costs. If it were the case that the effect of training on task-switching was smaller than its impact on learning transfer, then indeed, a larger sample size would be required to observe this difference. However, if this were the case, it would suggest that learning transfer and task-switching are not directly (and commonly) mediated by the strength of associations between task-sets. Rather, even if the learned associations between task-sets are comparable across situations that require learning transfer or task-switching, other factors exist to influence performance during task-switching, over and above the influence of associations between task-sets. This is in-line with recent proposals that the negotiation between stable and flexible performance may occur at multiple levels of information processing (Dreisbach et al., 2024), (although see Egner, 2023, for arguments for the independence of stability and flexibility). The current study is the first, to our knowledge, to probe relationships between conflict-proof performance and flexibility across multiple cognitive operations (transfer and switching) within one paradigm. Regardless of the interpretation of why there was a lack of group difference in task-switching performance in Experiment Two, the current null result speaks against a direct relationship between learning transfer and task-switching when training modulates the relationships between constituent tasks.

General Discussion

Over two experiments, we sought to determine the influence of contextual clarity on the use of task-sets during learning transfer and task-switching. In Experiment One, we showed that rarely switching between tasks during training hindered performance on a novel task, when that task required the mixing of behavioural subsets from both trained tasks. In contrast, rare switching during training did not hinder the reapplication of all behaviours from a single trained task to a novel task. Under the assumption that rare switching delineates task contexts (Flesch et al., 2018 (Flesch et al., , 2022;; Gershman et al., 2013; Niv, 2019), this finding supports the hypothesis that greater contextual clarity better segregates task representations, thereby impairing participants' ability to combine and associate elements of these separate tasks in the transfer context. In Experiment Two, we determined whether such training induces another anticipated consequence of attenuated representational sharing: reduced between-task interference during task-switching. In contrast to the hypothesis that the conditions that diminish learning transfer should also impact task-switching, we did not observe an influence of training on task-switching performance. This was despite the elicitation of behaviours during the training phase that were comparable to Experiment One, a robust elicitation of switch costs in the test phase, and a large sample that matched that of Experiment One. Whether this finding calls into question the assumed relationship between learning transfer and task-switching is discussed further below.

Both experiments demonstrated the strengths of the current paradigm for assessing how cross-task associations influence learning transfer and task-switching. Across both experiments, training manipulated the extent to which behaviours from Task A and Task B were mixed when performing either task. This provides a clear proxy for how often information was shared across tasks. Further, frequent switching during training selectively increased how often cross-task information was used, rather than disrupting task knowledge generally. Task knowledge remained intact, as demonstrated by both training groups selecting very few never-relevant locations during the training and test phases of either experiment. Instead, the impact of training on learning transfer and task-switching could reflect the extent of association between learned task-sets. Future work should determine whether the training regimen modulated associations between items belonging to each task-set (Lee et al., 2022), invoked a strategy of switching more frequently between tasks (Fröber & Dreisbach, 2017), or conditioned preparedness to switch between task-sets (Braem, 2017). However, whether the latter could occur without influencing task-switching performance would also need to be investigated. Regardless of the precise mechanisms of association that are modulated during training, the current paradigm can provide insight into the sources of cognitive challenge during task-switching (Dreisbach & Fröber, 2019), while the consistent behavioural effects of the training regimen allow us to explore how task-set associations, in turn, impact learning transfer and task-switching.

The question then becomes, how did the type of training impact task representations in a way that hampered learning transfer in one case, but spared task-switching in the other? If learning transfer and task-switching benefit from opposite approaches to information sharing between learned tasks (Garner & Dux, 2023; Musslick & Cohen, 2021; Musslick et al., 2019), how might training designed to modulate information sharing affect one and not the other? One possibility is that the training manipulation did not influence overlap between task sets. For instance, frequent switching could increase the association between Task A and Task B without introducing Task B information into the Task A representation. If we have not modulated the extent of overlap between task-sets, then the current findings may not directly answer the question of whether information overlap reflects a common component to learning transfer and task-switching. There are multiple reasons to suspect that the training regimen did successfully manipulate the extent of separability/overlap between the two trained task-sets. Along with the behavioural data from the training phase outlined above, which show mixing of Task A and B behaviours within Task A trials (and vice versa), the current paradigm was constructed to ensure that both the visual environment and response modality were the same across task-sets, which theoretically ensures a baseline level of information sharing (Petri et al., 2021). Further, previous work shows that rare switches between tasks attenuate common information in the neural activity that corresponds to each task, even when tasks are performed in the same visual environment (Flesch et al., 2022). However, it is also possible that more frequent switching during training induced a pre-emptive policy of switching or a learned readiness to switch between tasks (Braem, 2017; Geddert & Egner, 2024; Musslick et al., 2019), without the task representations overlapping.

Thus, it is useful to ask whether readiness to switch could increase without also modulating what information is encoded into the neural signal for each task. Understanding this will help determine how far the current findings inform the proposed relationships between learning transfer and task-switching.

The observation that the rare switching experienced by the Stable group did impair mixing of cross-task components during transfer in Experiment One suggests that the training manipulation impacted some level of integration between the two task sets. Indeed, previous work has shown that novel task performance is faster when task components share an associative relationship. Lee et al. (2022) trained participants to perform strategically paired stimulus-response tasks over blocks (e.g. A&B, B&C, D&E). Participants subsequently showed better performance when faced with novel pairings that shared an indirect association (A&C) relative to those that did not (A&D). This was taken as evidence that indirect associations between task components facilitate their groupings into novel task sets. The current results extend these findings by showing that frequent switching, or close temporal proximity between tasks, is sufficient to increase cross-task integration -here, integration happened without an explicit pairing of task A and B components. Given that, at the neural level, associative strength is reflected by a greater propensity for relevant neurons to fire together (Hebb, 2005), we can assume that more frequent switching altered task representations so that they were more likely to contain neural information related to the other task. Thus, considering the cognitive processes that underpinned changes in cross-task associability, and how these changes impacted performance at test, may constrain the conditions under which a relationship between learning transfer and task-switching might occur.

One possibility is that training modulated task representations by impacting expectations about the utility of the task that was not currently being performed. As the colour cues were removed in the training phase, task-switches were optimally detected by exhausting the locations from the previously successful task; that is, if the last target was found in a Task A location, then exhausting Task A locations provides definitive evidence that the task has switched. Thus, the Variable group would be required to select more than four doors (under the optimal policy) more frequently than the Stable group. Further, the probability that the task has switched increases with each failure to reveal a target in a Task A location. It is possible that failures to reveal the target were interpreted as errors, and that the increased errors experienced by the Variable group resulted in them overweighting recent errors. This would inflate estimates of the probability that the task had switched. In line with this interpretation, more frequent switching of rules on a Wisconsin card sorting task results in greater reliance on recent experiences, compared to rare switching between rules (Wen et al., 2023). Alternately, it could be that more frequent switching during training induced a strategic choice to switch more often (c.f. Fröber & Dreisbach, 2017).

Either way, this would result in stronger anticipatory excitation of Task B behaviours during performance of Task A (and vice versa), for the Variable compared to the Stable group. Such a process would presumably cause more cross-task selections, if excitation was strong enough to influence behaviour. Excitation of cross-task behaviours could facilitate performance in the Mixed transfer condition, which combined two locations each from Task A and Task B. If the first discovered target location was from Task A, then the concurrent excitation of Task B behaviours would bring those behaviours closer to threshold for selection. Thus, the Variable group would be more ready to select Task B behaviours on the Mixed transfer task than the Stable group. In contrast, the Stable group should be at an advantage in the Identity transfer condition (which consisted of all the locations from one of Task A or Task B), as the appropriate strategy is to select locations from only the task that matches the first discovered target location. Presumably, reduced cross-task associations would be beneficial under these circumstances. In line with this interpretation, the Stable group were numerically faster to learn in the Identity condition compared to the Variable group (and slower to learn in the Mixed condition compared to the Variable group). However, although the current results showed a significant Group x Transfer Type interaction, we did not observe that the groups were statistically different at each level of transfer. This is likely due to the high accuracy on the transfer tasks overall. Future research efforts should seek to make transfer tasks more challenging, to ensure sufficient variability in knowledge onset. This would enable us to determine whether separating tasks in time (rare switching) does confer greater advantage for Identity transfer, compared to mixing them together in time (frequent switching), as is predicted by this account.

If more frequent switching during training increased the salience of the task not currently being performed, why was there no discernable impact of training on task-switching in Experiment Two? Indeed, greater excitation of cross-task behaviours are the very conditions that should modulate task-switching costs; either via incurring greater control demands, thereby increasing costs (Cools, 2019; Musslick & Cohen, 2021), or by reducing the time required to switch between tasks (Bustos et al., 2024; Dreisbach & Fröber, 2019). These positions can be reconciled with the current results if we assume that reintroducing explicit colour cues in the task-switching phase of Experiment Two negated the salience of cross-task behaviours acquired by frequent switching during training. The colour cues explicitly signal that there is zero probability that the target is in a cross-task location. Thus, the association between tasks observed during training can be safely ignored. In this case, learned cross-task associations could impact task-switching, but only where task probability is similarly uncertain.

This interpretation aligns with previous suggestions that the control settings governing task-switching performance are learned (Held et al., 2024) and context dependent (Dreisbach & Haider, 2006; Geddert & Egner, 2024; Musslick et al., 2019; Siqi-Liu & Egner, 2020). However, both task-switching and learning transfer tests involved reintroduced colour cues. This begs the question of why it interrupted the impact of training for task-switching, but not learning transfer. In Experiment One, the colour cues at test signalled two new unknown tasks. Further, they were presented in blocks, so there was little need to attend to the colour trial by trial in order to perform the current task. Thus, in Experiment One, the colour cues did not signal when it was time to update behaviour. In contrast, the cues in the task-switching phase resolved uncertainty about the task state, and consequently signalled when it was time to adjust expectations about which behaviours would uncover the target. Under this view, the information offered by environmental cues about cross-task relevance may be the factor that determines whether or not learned cross-task associations will impact performance across the cognitive domains of learning transfer or task switching. Further, this interpretation suggests that the task-sets underpinning learning transfer and task-switching can be rapidly reconfigured in response to the information conveyed by task cues. Further work is required to test this possibility.

It is also possible that the current training regimen was too short to induce changes that would influence task-switching performance. It has recently been shown that contextual cues that perfectly predict a high or low probability of a task-switch, such as a background screen, can influence switch-costs between classification tasks requiring a single response (e.g. whether a presented item is a piece of clothing or not), but only after multiple days of training (Xu et al., 2024). It has been proposed on the basis of such findings that durable changes to task-switching performance cannot be achieved with short-term adaptations to environmental statistics, but rather require a neural reconfiguration that can only be attained with extended learning (Braem et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2026). Relatedly, such extended training regimens have been shown to increase neural dissimilarity between tasks while also reducing multitasking costs (Garner & Dux, 2015; Mueckstein et al., 2025), reinforcing the assumed connections between task-overlap, dual-task interference, and task-switching. It is of interest to determine whether increasing the duration of the current training regimen would serve to impact task-switch costs, and whether or not this increased duration maintains, exacerbates, or negates the impact of training on learning transfer.

Regardless of whether consistent environmental cues or extended training are required to induce changes to task-switching performance, the current results are the first (to our knowledge) to directly speak to the links between two separate but related hypothesised trade-offs discussed in the cognitive control literature. Increased overlap in underlying task-representations has been assumed to foster learning efficiency while harming multitasking performance (see Garner & Dux, 2023; Musslick & Cohen, 2021, for reviews). Such overlap is also assumed to induce a neural state that invokes greater control demands (i.e.

greater relative suppression of the competing task) during task-switching (Musslick & Cohen, 2019; Musslick et al., 2018). The extent to which control is applied has also been hypothesised to underlie a stability (conflict-proof) vs flexibility (reduced costs) trade-off that is adapted according to experience (e.g. Braem, 2017; Xu et al., 2024) or current task demands (Fröber et al., 2018; Geddert & Egner, 2024; Qiao et al., 2023). Despite the apparent connections between these trade-offs, our current results show that short-term training that perturbs task boundaries (by increasing task-mixing) is sufficient to impact learning transfer, but is not sufficient to impact task-switching. Importantly, task-knowledge remained intact in both groups. This provides initial evidence that the brain can readily draw from additional prior task experiences to impact learning efficiency, yet can retain a strong enough representation of the original task-set so that task-switching is not perturbed. This accords with arguments that task-switching performance is dependent on the fidelity of task-representations in a cognitive map that underpins long-term memory representations (Mayr & Grätz, 2024; Mayr et al., 2014). Future work should determine whether the current training manipulation, which required tracking progress on one task to determine the utility of a second task, also impacts multitasking performance (attempting to perform both tasks simultaneously). Such a test would require a modified setup of the current paradigm but would inform whether learning efficiency and multitasking are engaged by dissociable processes to those that govern the stability vs flexibility trade-off, or whether theories regarding learning efficiency and multitasking should be constrained to refer to specific forms of learning -such as the acquisition of a single stimulus-response mapping, and not the multi-component tasks that were learned here.

These findings also speak to previous mixed results regarding the influence of contextual clarity on underlying task representations. In the training phase, reducing contextual clarity (by frequently switching between tasks) increased the likelihood that behaviours from both tasks were performed during performance of a single task. This supports previous observations that a lack of contextual clarity blurs the boundaries of what constitutes a task set (Gershman et al., 2013; Niv, 2019; Niv et al., 2015). This stands in contrast to the hypothesis that increased competition between tasks may help dissociate representations, in order to perform multiple tasks more efficiently (Musslick & Cohen, 2021; Musslick et al., 2020; Sagiv et al., 2020). However, the current task-sets involve multiple responses, whereas the latter theories have largely considered tasks that require a single response. Further work is required to determine whether rare switching always promotes dissociated task representations, or whether this is partly dependent on the task being performed.

Conclusions

Over two experiments, we manipulated the extent to which two tasks were associated with one another, by controlling the rate of covert task-state switches during training. Rare switching reduced cross-task interference during performance of a single task, compared to more frequent switching. This reduced interference facilitated replication of a whole learned task in novel circumstances, but limited the ability to combine components of learned tasks to form a novel task representation, presumably because of weak associations between the tasks. Thus, the extent to which shared task information supports transfer depends on the learned associations between task sets. The same manipulation did not impact task-switching, even though the reduced association between tasks should theoretically ameliorate switch costs. This may be due to rapidly updated cross-task associations when contextual cues are clear. Thus, information sharing between task representations may flexibly shift with the context.

Constraints on generality.

The findings reported here are based on two experiments conducted with predominantly university-aged participants, which limits the generalizability of the results to groups of other ages or education levels. Further, the lab-based nature of the current tasks may not fully reflect the complexity of learning transfer and task-switching in real-world scenarios.

Public significance statement. Context helps us determine which past experiences are relevant in a given situation. This study shows that when different tasks are experienced in clearly separated contexts, people become better at keeping those tasks distinct, but less able to combine information from them when faced with a new challenge. In contrast, frequently interleaving tasks encourages people to link information across experiences, which supports learning in situations that require recombining previously acquired knowledge. Surprisingly, however, the same training experiences did not influence people's ability to switch between the original tasks when clear task cues were available. These findings suggest that the way experiences are organised over time shapes how knowledge is generalised to new situations, but that learning transfer and task-switching may rely on partly distinct cognitive mechanisms. More broadly, the results highlight how the structure of our everyday experiences can influence whether we learn flexible skills that transfer across contexts or develop more specialised knowledge tied to particular situations.
